los.text: Describe the main causes, pathophysiology, clinical signs and symptoms and principles of treatment of a collapsed patient
sessions: Clin 3: Principles of treatment of cardiac arrythmia
los.html:
• Syncope = transient LOC from global cerebral hypoperfusion, rapid onset, short, spontaneous full recovery.
TypeFeatures
Reflex (vasovagal)
  • Commonest.
  • Triggers: standing, heat, pain, emotion
  • Prodrome (sweating, nausea, tunnel vision)
  • Brief jerks possible
  • Quick recovery.
  • Also situational (cough, micturition) and carotid sinus hypersensitivity
Orthostatic
  • On standing.
  • Drugs (antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates), hypovolaemia, autonomic failure (diabetes, Parkinson's).
  • Lying/standing BP: fall ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic within 3 min
Cardiac
  • Exertional or supine syncope, no prodrome, palpitations, FHx sudden death.
  • Arrhythmia (VT, complete heart block, sick sinus, long QT, Brugada) or structural (aortic stenosis, HOCM, PE)
DifferentialsSeizure (tongue biting, post-ictal confusion, prolonged jerking), hypoglycaemia, stroke/TIA (rarely causes LOC), psychogenic.
Ix12-lead ECG for all, lying/standing BP, glucose, FBC/U&E; echo if murmur; ambulatory ECG/implantable loop recorder; tilt table.
Treatment
  • Reflex → reassurance, avoid triggers, counter-pressure manoeuvres, fluids/salt.
  • Orthostatic → review drugs, fluids, compression, fludrocortisone/midodrine.
  • Bradyarrhythmia → pacemaker
  • VT → treat cause, ICD
  • Tachyarrhythmias → rate/rhythm control, ablation.
  • Structural → e.g. valve replacement.
Collapse with no outputALS: CPR, shockable (VF/pVT) vs non-shockable (PEA/asystole), reversible causes (4Hs and 4Ts).
Red flags (urgent cardiology): exertional syncope, ECG abnormality, heart failure, new murmur, FHx sudden cardiac death <40, syncope while lying down.

los.text: Explain the pathophysiology, diagnosis and principles of treatment of coronary artery disease (CAD), focussing on angina and acute coronary syndrome
sessions: Clin 2: Coronary artery disease / ACS pathophysiology
los.html:
• Atherosclerosis narrows coronary arteries.
  • Stable angina: fixed stenosis (usually >70%)
  • → supply/demand mismatch on exertion
  • → central chest tightness radiating to arm/jaw, relieved by rest/GTN within minutes.
ACS
  • Plaque rupture/erosion → platelet aggregation + thrombus.
  • Unstable angina: rest/crescendo pain, no troponin rise.
  • NSTEMI: partial occlusion → subendocardial infarction; ↑ troponin; ECG ST depression/T inversion or normal.
  • STEMI: complete occlusion → transmural infarction; ST elevation or new LBBB.
Dx
  • History, ECG, high-sensitivity troponin (0 and 1–3 h), CXR, bloods (lipids, HbA1c).
  • Stable chest pain: CT coronary angiography first line (NICE), functional imaging, invasive angiography.
Stable angina Rx
  • GTN PRN
  • β-blocker or rate-limiting CCB
  • Then combine/add long-acting nitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil, ranolazine.
  • Secondary prevention: aspirin 75 mg, statin (atorvastatin 80 mg), ACEi if diabetes/HTN.
  • Revascularisation (PCI/CABG) if symptoms persist.
STEMIAspirin 300 mg, primary PCI if within 12 h and possible within 120 min (otherwise fibrinolysis), plus second antiplatelet (prasugrel/ticagrelor), anticoagulation.
NSTEMIAspirin + antithrombin (fondaparinux), risk stratify (GRACE) → angiography within 72 h if intermediate/high risk.
Morphine/O₂ only if needed (O₂ if sats <94%).

los.text: Explain the changes in cardiac conduction that lead to alterations in the ECG, cardiac rhythm and symptoms
los.html:
Sinus bradycardia/tachycardiaNormal P before every QRS.
AV block
  • 1st degree (PR >200 ms)
  • 2nd degree Mobitz I/Wenckebach (PR lengthens until a dropped beat; AV node, often benign)
  • Mobitz II (sudden dropped beats with fixed PR; infranodal, risk of complete block → pacing)
  • 3rd degree/complete (P and QRS dissociated; broad escape rhythm; syncope = Stokes–Adams).
Bundle branch blockQRS ≥120 ms. RBBB (RSR′ in V1, "MaRRoW"), LBBB (W in V1, M in V6, "WiLLiaM"; new LBBB + chest pain = treat as MI).
Atrial fibrillationChaotic atrial activity → irregularly irregular, no P waves. Symptoms: palpitations, breathlessness, stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc).
Atrial flutterMacro re-entry; sawtooth waves ~300/min, often 2:1 block → HR ~150.
SVT (AVNRT/AVRT)Re-entry; narrow regular tachycardia. WPW: accessory pathway → short PR + delta wave.
VTBroad complex tachycardia → haemodynamic collapse, VF. VF: chaotic, no output.
Long QTTorsades de pointes (drugs, ↓K⁺, ↓Mg²⁺, congenital).
MechanismsAbnormal automaticity, triggered activity (after-depolarisations), re-entry, conduction block.
SymptomsPalpitations, dizziness, syncope, breathlessness, chest pain, heart failure; sudden death.

los.text: Describe the structure and functions of the heart, including chambers, valves and coronary circulation
los.html:
Chambers
  • Right atrium (SVC, IVC, coronary sinus in)
  • → tricuspid
  • → right ventricle
  • → pulmonary valve
  • → pulmonary trunk
  • → lungs
  • → pulmonary veins
  • → left atrium
  • → mitral (bicuspid)
  • → left ventricle (thickest wall)
  • → aortic valve
  • → aorta.
  • AV valves have chordae tendineae + papillary muscles (prevent eversion).
  • Semilunar valves have three cusps
  • Aortic sinuses give rise to coronary arteries.
Right coronary artery (RCA)
  • RA, RV, inferior LV, posterior septum
  • Supplies SA node (~60%) and AV node (~80–90%) → inferior MI may cause bradycardia/heart block.
  • Branches: marginal, posterior descending (in right-dominant hearts, ~70%).
Left main stemLAD (anterior LV, anterior ⅔ of septum, apex) + circumflex (lateral LV, LA).
Venous drainageGreat, middle and small cardiac veins → coronary sinus → RA. Thebesian veins drain directly.
Coronary perfusion of LV occurs mainly in diastole (compression during systole), so tachycardia ↓ perfusion time.
ECG territoriesInferior (II, III, aVF: RCA), anterior (V1–V4: LAD), lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6: circumflex).

los.text: Describe the timing and events of the cardiac cycle
los.html:
Atrial systole"atrial kick" tops up ventricles (~20% of filling; lost in AF). a wave in JVP. Late diastole.
Isovolumetric contractionVentricles contract, AV valves close (S1), all valves shut, pressure rises fast. c wave.
Ventricular ejectionVentricular pressure exceeds aortic/pulmonary → semilunar valves open; stroke volume ~70 mL (EF ~55–70%).
Isovolumetric relaxationSemilunar valves close (S2: A2 then P2; physiological splitting on inspiration). Dicrotic notch on aortic trace.
Ventricular filling
  • AV valves open
  • → rapid passive filling (S3 if abnormal in adults: HF, volume overload)
  • → diastasis
  • → atrial systole (S4: stiff ventricle).
JVPa (atrial contraction), c (tricuspid bulging), x descent (atrial relaxation), v (atrial filling against closed tricuspid), y descent (tricuspid opens).
TimingSystole ~0.3 s; diastole ~0.5 s at 75 bpm. Tachycardia shortens diastole most.
PressuresLV 120/0–10, aorta 120/80, RV 25/0–5, PA 25/10.

los.text: Describe the components of the conducting system of the heart and trace the pathway of normal conduction through the heart and relate to a normal ECG
sessions: BMS 3: Electrical changes in the heart and ECG
los.html:
Pathway
  • SA node (RA near SVC; pacemaker ~60–100/min)
  • → atrial muscle (internodal tracts)
  • → AV node (delay ~0.1 s lets ventricles fill)
  • → bundle of His
  • → left and right bundle branches (left → anterior and posterior fascicles)
  • → Purkinje fibres
  • → ventricular myocardium (endocardium → epicardium, apex → base).
Pacemaker potential
  • Slow depolarisation via funny current (If, HCN channels) then Ca²⁺ influx (L-type).
  • Sympathetic ↑ slope (↑ HR)
  • Vagal ACh hyperpolarises (↓ HR).
Ventricular action potentialPhase 0 Na⁺ influx, 1 early repolarisation (K⁺ out), 2 plateau (Ca²⁺ in, K⁺ out), 3 repolarisation (K⁺), 4 resting.
ECG partRepresentsNormal
P waveAtrial depolarisation<0.12 s
PR intervalAtrial depolarisation + AV node delay0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares)
QRSVentricular depolarisation<0.12 s
ST segmentPlateau (ventricles fully depolarised)Isoelectric
T waveVentricular repolarisationUpright in most leads
QTcDepolarisation + repolarisation<440 ms (men), <460 ms (women)
  • Atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS.
    • Paper speed 25 mm/s: 1 small square = 0.04 s
    • HR = 300 / number of large squares between R waves.

los.text: Explain how blood pressure is normally maintained
los.html:
MAP = CO × TPR, where CO = HR × SV. MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓ pulse pressure.
Short term (seconds) – baroreceptor reflex
  • Carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) stretch receptors
  • → NTS in medulla. ↓ BP
  • → ↓ firing
  • → ↑ sympathetic (↑ HR, contractility, vasoconstriction, venoconstriction) and ↓ vagal tone.
  • Resets in chronic hypertension.
Medium term – hormonal
  • RAAS (↓ renal perfusion/↓ Na⁺ at macula densa/sympathetic β1 → renin → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction, aldosterone, ADH, thirst)
  • ADH (vasoconstriction via V1, water retention via V2)
  • ANP/BNP (stretch → natriuresis, vasodilation)
  • Adrenaline.
Long term – renalPressure natriuresis, blood volume control (Guyton).
LocalAutoregulation (myogenic response), metabolites (adenosine, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺), endothelium (NO, prostacyclin vs endothelin).
Stroke volume depends on preload (Frank–Starling), contractility, afterload.

los.text: Describe the normal histological structures of the heart and common pathologies
los.html:
LayersEndocardium (endothelium, subendocardial layer with Purkinje fibres), myocardium, epicardium (visceral pericardium with fat and coronary vessels).
Cardiomyocytes
  • Branched, central nucleus (1–2), striated
  • Joined by intercalated discs (desmosomes/fascia adherens for mechanical coupling, gap junctions for electrical coupling).
  • Abundant mitochondria.
  • Atrial myocytes have granules (ANP).
Purkinje fibresLarge, pale (glycogen-rich), few myofibrils.
ValvesAvascular fibrous core covered by endothelium.

Common pathologies

Myocardial infarction (time course)
  • 0–4 h no visible change (wavy fibres)
  • → 4–24 h coagulative necrosis, neutrophils from ~24 h
  • → 3–7 days macrophages (rupture risk, days 3–7)
  • → 1–2 weeks granulation tissue
  • → >2 months dense scar.
Hypertrophy(HTN, aortic stenosis)Large myocytes with "boxcar" nuclei.
Myocarditis (viral, lymphocytic infiltrate), cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic: myocyte disarray), rheumatic heart disease (Aschoff bodies, Anitschkow cells), amyloid, infective endocarditis (vegetations).
